rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Moses drove the locusts away by pointing east and west, but Haman prevented Pharaoh from releasing the Israelites.
rows.anchor: فأشار بعصاه نحو المشرق والمغرب فرجعت الجراد من حيث جاءت حتى كأن لم تكن قط، ولم يدع هامان فرعون أن يخلي عن بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third plague was qمل, dated to year three by Ali ibn Ibrahim and month three by other exegetes; it was tiny wingless locusts that destroyed crops.
rows.anchor: في السنة الثالثة - في رواية علي بن إبراهيم - وفي الشهر الثالث - عن غيره من المفسرين - القمل

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr identifies qمل as grain weevils; the infestation also devastated the grain yield.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير القمل السوس الذي يخرج من الحبوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The insects tormented bodies and sleep; Pharaoh promised to release Israel if Moses removed them, but after seven days and relief he reneged.
rows.anchor: ومنعتهم النوم والقرار فصرخوا وصاحوا وقال فرعون لموسى ادع لنا ربك لئن كشفت عنا القمل لأكفن عن بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth plague, dated to year four or month four, was frogs that filled homes, food, drink, and cooking pots and made ordinary life intolerable.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله عليهم في السنة الرابعة - وقيل في الشهر الرابع - الضفادع فكانت تكون في طعامهم وشرابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people vowed repentance, faith, and Israel's release; Moses secured their pledges, the frogs vanished after seven days, and they broke the covenant.
rows.anchor: فإنا نؤمن بك ونرسل معك بني إسرائيل فأخذ عهودهم ومواثيقهم ثم دعا ربه فكشف عنهم الضفادع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fifth year's blood plague made Nile water blood to Egyptians but water to Israelites, and even water poured into an Egyptian's mouth turned to blood.
rows.anchor: فسأل ماء النيل عليهم دما فكان القبطي يراه دما، والإسرائيلي يراه ماء فإذا شربه الإسرائيلي كان ماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blood lasted seven days; Egyptians could neither eat nor drink anything but blood, and Pharaoh's thirst persisted even when chewing moist plants.
rows.anchor: فمكثوا في ذلك سبعة أيام لا يأكلون إلا الدم، ولا يشربون إلا الدم

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the blood plague was nosebleeds; after Moses prayed for its removal, Pharaoh's people again failed to believe or release Israel.
rows.anchor: قال زيد بن أسلم الدم الذي سلط عليهم كان الرعاف فأتوا موسى فقالوا ادع لنا ربك

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report from Abu ʿAbd Allah identifies the affliction called الرجْز in the plea as snow and calls Khurasan a land of that affliction.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عبد الله عليه السلام لئن كشف عنا الرجز لنؤمنن لك، قال الرجز هو الثلج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the snow report does not fit the verse particularly well.
rows.anchor: والرواية لا تنطبق على الآية ذاك الانطباق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 2:51 gives the total forty nights as appointed, while 7:142 explains that total as two appointments: thirty nights followed by ten more to complete it.
rows.anchor: آية البقرة تدل على أن مجموع الأربعين كان عن مواعدة، وآية الأعراف على أن ما في آية البقرة مجموع المواعدتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointment is expressed in nights rather than days because night better suits communion with God: the senses are gathered and the soul is more ready for intimacy.
rows.anchor: لأن الميقات كان للتقرب إلى الله سبحانه ومناجاته وذكره، وذلك أخص بالليل وأنسب لما فيه من اجتماع الحواس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointment's blessing included the Torah's descent; Qur'an 73:1 and 73:5-7 likewise associate night vigil with reception of weighty speech.
rows.anchor: وقد كان من بركات هذا الميقات نزول التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary seeing is bodily and requires materiality in both seer and seen, whereas Qur'anic teaching makes God unlike anything, without body, place, time, direction, or a comparable image; bodily sight cannot reach Him.
rows.anchor: الرؤية والإبصار يحتاج إلى عمل طبيعي في جهاز الإبصار يهيئ للباصر صوره مماثلة لصورة الجسم المبصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses could not have been ignorant that God is beyond bodily perception or imagined that a material faculty could see the immaterial; his request and God's reply concern a non-ocular kind of vision.
rows.anchor: فإن كان موسى يسأل الرؤية فإنما سأل غير هذه الرؤية البصرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls direct awareness of something as actually present to the self a kind of vision, including awareness of one's self, inner faculties, and inward states without bodily or spatial conditions.
rows.anchor: وتسمية هذا القسم من العلم الذي يجد فيه الإنسان نفس المعلوم بواقعيته الخارجية رؤية مطردة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's being witness to and encompassing everything means any meeting with Him would be immediate and non-local, not sensory face-to-face encounter.
rows.anchor: فلو وجده شيء لوجده على ظاهر كل شيء وباطنه وعلى نفس وجدانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 'the heart did not deny what it saw,' heart means the perceiving human soul, not the pineal-shaped flesh in the chest.
rows.anchor: من نسبة الرؤيه إلى الفؤاد الذي لا شبهه في كون المراد به هو النفس الإنسانية الشاعرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stain of sins veils people's selves from their Lord; if they saw Him, they would do so with their hearts, not their eyes.
rows.anchor: فحجبهم عن تشريف المشاهدة، ولو رأوه لرأوه بقلوبهم أي أنفسهم لا بأبصارهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an affirms another vision beyond sense organs, including seeing Hell with certainty and Abraham's vision of the kingdom of heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقد أثبت الله سبحانه في موارد من كلامه قسما آخر من الرؤية وراء رؤية الجارحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kingdom Abraham saw is the inward reality of things, rather than their sensory outward appearance; this supports a non-sensory kind of vision and immediate awareness of God.
rows.anchor: الملكوت هو باطن الأشياء لا ظاهرها المحسوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People have direct awareness of God beyond belief reached by inference; self-absorption and sins distract from it, producing heedlessness rather than erasing the underlying knowledge.
rows.anchor: فليس في كلامه تعالى ما يشعر بذلك البتة بل عبر عن هذا الجهل بالغفلة وهي زوال العلم بالعلم لا زوال أصل العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reason and reports from the Imams of the Prophet's household support this account of vision.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده العقل بساطع براهينه، وكذا ما ورد من الأخبار عن إئمة أهل البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous attain this vision and meeting on the Day of Resurrection; in earthly life people remain occupied with bodily needs and are still striving toward their Lord.
rows.anchor: أن هذا العلم المسمى بالرؤية واللقاء يتم للصالحين من عباد الله يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's recognition of error chronologically follows Moses' return, as Surah Ta-Ha details, but is placed beside the calf episode to keep their regret and grief close to the act that prompted them.
rows.anchor: والآية أعني قوله { ولما سقط } بحسب المعنى مترتب على الآيات التالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The regret statement is also placed here because it is itself prayer-like, while the next verse's ending recounts Moses praying for himself and Aaron.
rows.anchor: ولذا لما ذكر اتخاذهم العجل في الآية الأولى وصله بندامتهم وحسرتهم في الآية الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asaf means intense anger and grief; khilafa is taking up a predecessor's responsibility, and ʿajala means seeking something before its proper time, following al-Raghib's definition.
rows.anchor: الأسف بكسر السين صفة مشبهة من الأسف وهو شدة الغضب والحزن والخلافة القيام بالأمر بعد غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses returned angry after God told him that his people had gone astray; he reproached them for badly succeeding him and hastening their Lord's affair.
rows.anchor: ولما رجع موسى إلى قومه وهو في حال غضب وأسف لما أخبره الله تعالى لدى الرجوع بأن قومه ضلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred reading is that they sought prematurely the Lord's promised affair at Moses' appointment, namely the Torah's descent; God's wise plan is unaffected by human haste or demand.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد بأمر ربهم أمره الذي لاجله واعد موسى لميقاته، وهو نزول التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One alternative reads the rebuke as asking whether they worshipped the calf before a command from their Lord arrived.
rows.anchor: وربما قيل إن معنى { أعجلتم أمر ربكم } أعجلتم بعبادة العجل قبل أن يأتيكم أمر من ربكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another alternative says they expected God's reward for worship, and turned to another object of worship when it did not arrive.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى استعجلتم وعد الله وثوابه على عبادته فلما لم تنالوه عدلتم إلى عبادة غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third alternative says they presumed Moses' appointment had ended and changed their practice rather than waiting for his return as God commanded.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى أعجلتم عما أمركم به ربكم وهو انتظار رجوع موسى حافظين لعهده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses threw down the Torah tablets and seized Aaron by the head, dragging him toward himself; Ta-Ha recounts Moses asking why Aaron did not follow the people when they strayed.
rows.anchor: وكذا ما فعله موسى بأخيه من أخذ رأسه يجره إليه كأنه مقدمة لضربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron's address 'son of my mother' instead of 'brother' or 'son of my father' softens Moses and stirs his compassion.
rows.anchor: وإنما خاطبه بذكر أمهما دون أن يقول يا أخي أو يا ابن أبي للترقيق وتهييج الرحمة

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Aaron says the people overpowered him and nearly killed him because he opposed their calf worship; he asks Moses not to let enemies gloat or count him among wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: إن القوم استضعفوني وكادوا يقتلونني } لما خالفتهم في أمر العجل ومنعتهم عن عبادته

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Aaron explains in Ta-Ha that he feared Moses would accuse him of dividing the Israelites and disregarding his instruction.
rows.anchor: إني خشيت أن تقول فرقت بين بني إسرائيل ولم ترقب قولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context indicates Moses was angry at Aaron too, believing he had not resisted the Israelites enough, though Aaron had judged restraint better for communal welfare.
rows.anchor: وظاهر سياق الآية وكذا ما في سورة طه من آيات القصة أن موسى غضب على هارون كما غضب على بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Different temperaments and practical judgments between two infallible prophets are possible: infallibility governs divine rulings, not dispositions or ways of life.
rows.anchor: وهذا المقدار من الاختلاف في السليقة والمشيئة بين نبيين معصومين لا دليل على منعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses took Aaron's head as if preparing to strike him because he thought Aaron had acted independently; this was discipline over advisory judgment, not punishment for violating a binding command, and Aaron was right.
rows.anchor: فما وقع منه إنما هو تأديب في أمر إرشادي لا عقاب في أمر مولوي وإن كان الحق في ذلك مع هارون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says Moses handled Aaron as people handle themselves in anger, gripping a beard or biting a lip, because he regarded his brother as himself.
rows.anchor: أن موسى إنما فعل ذلك مستعظما لفعلهم مفكرا فيما كان منهم كما يفعل الإنسان ذلك بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another alternative says Moses displayed his anger at the Israelites' apostasy to show its gravity and deter future conduct.
rows.anchor: أنه أراد أن يظهر ما اعتراه من الغضب على قومه لإكباره منهم ما صاروا وإليه من الكفر والارتداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says Moses pulled Aaron close to consult him privately and ask what had happened.
rows.anchor: أنه إنما جره إلى نفسه ليناجيه ويستفسر حال القوم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth explanation says Moses took Aaron's head compassionately because Aaron shared his grief, while Aaron feared people would mistake the gesture for insult.
rows.anchor: أنه لما رأى أن بهارون مثل ما به من الغضب والأسف أخذ برأسه متوجعا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says most or all of these alternative explanations do not fit the passage's context.
rows.anchor: وجل هذه الوجوه أو كلها لا تلائم سياق الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening says Moses already knew of the people's apostasy before seeing them, because God told him at the appointment, as Ta-Ha recounts.
rows.anchor: وقوله في صدر الآية { ولما رجع موسى إلى قومه غضبان أسفا } يدل على أنه كان عالما بأمر ارتداد قومه من قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Moses knew of the apostasy, anger manifested when he saw the people: knowledge produces grief, while witnessing the offender enables defensive or retaliatory action; seeing an event alone differs from seeing it with others.
rows.anchor: لأن للعلم حكما وللمشاهدة حكما آخر، والغضب هيجان القوة الدافعة للدفع أو الانتقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' prayer asks forgiveness for himself and Aaron; forgiveness has a broader scope than sin, as discussed earlier in the work.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم في الكلام على المغفرة في آخر الجزء السادس من الكتاب أن المغفرة أعم موردا من المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite 'anger' and 'humiliation' signal their magnitude, while the verse leaves their precise referents unspecified.
rows.anchor: للإشعار بعظمتهما وقد أبهم الله سبحانه ما سينالهم من غضبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible referents include destruction of the calf and its drowning, expulsion of Samiri and killing some Israelites; or the people's abasement, killing, extermination, and captivity; alternatively, divine anger may mean punishment in the hereafter alongside worldly humiliation.
rows.anchor: فمن المحتمل أن تكون الإشارة بذلك إلى ما جرى عليهم بعد ذلك من تحريق العجل المعبود ونسفه في اليم نسفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending states a continuing divine rule: those who fabricate lies about God incur His anger and worldly humiliation, a principle also supported by rational inquiry.
rows.anchor: بظاهره يدل على أن ذلك أعني نيل غضب الرب سبحانه وذلة الحياة الدنيا سنة جارية إلهية في المفترين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first 'after it' refers to sins and the second to repentance; the verse's meaning is otherwise clear.
rows.anchor: ضمير { من بعدها } الأول راجع إلى السيئات، والثاني إلى التوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though general in wording, the repentance verse functions in this context as an exception for calf worshippers: genuine repentance from any sin can be accepted, as discussed under 4:17.
rows.anchor: فالتوبة إذا تحققت بحقيقة معناها في أية سيئة كانت لم يمنع من قبولها مانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses on the calf worshippers' punishment and repentance interrupt the narrative and address the Prophet; 'your Lord' and the retrospective wording signal this framing.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية والتي قبلها معترضتان في القصة، ووجه الخطاب فيهما إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 'when the anger fell silent from Moses,' رهبة means fear coupled with caution or self-protection.
rows.anchor: الرهبة هي خوف مع تحرز

rows.speaker: أبو واقد الليثي
rows.claim: Abu Waqid al-Laythi reports that on the way to Hunayn companions asked the Prophet for a tree shrine like the pagans' Dhāt Anwāṭ; he compared this to Israel asking Moses for a god and warned they followed earlier peoples' ways.
rows.anchor: عن أبي واقد الليثي قال خرجنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قبل حنين فمررنا بسدرة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عوف
rows.claim: A variant report attributed through Abdullah ibn Awf describes Dhāt Anwāṭ as a great sidr tree where weapons were hung and which was worshipped besides God.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عوف عن أبيه عن جده أن رجلا قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: In a report by Muhammad ibn Shahr Ashub, Ali answers the Head of the Jews' criticism by recalling that Israel asked for gods before their feet had dried after crossing the sea.
rows.anchor: فقال علي عليه السلام وأنتم لم تجف أقدامكم من ماء البحر حتى قلتم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reports that Moses planned thirty days away, God added ten, and the people assumed Moses had failed them after the first thirty before making the calf.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام قال إن موسى لما خرج وافدا إلى ربه واعدهم ثلاثين يوما

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jabir reports that God's speech to Moses at the mountain differed from the speech when He called him, likening its communicative force to ten thousand tongues and describing thunder as a close but imperfect analogy.
rows.anchor: لما كلم الله موسى يوم الطور كلمه بغير الكلام الذي كلمه يوم ناداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the thunder comparison is only an approximation and unobjectionable; the obscure 'ten thousand tongues' likely means the combined explanatory power of many tongues, so the difference is in how meaning is conveyed.
rows.anchor: ولعل المراد بقوة عشرة آلاف لسان ما في العشرة آلاف من قوة التفهيم لو تأيد بعضها ببعض

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: Ali argues that anything subject to eyesight is created and needs a creator, so bodily vision would make God a created being.
rows.anchor: فإن كل من جاز عليه البصر والرؤية فهو مخلوق، ولا بد للمخلوق من خالق

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: Imam al-Husayn reports Ali's answer: he did not worship a Lord unseen by eyes, but hearts see Him through faith; bodily sight would make God a created being likened to creation.
rows.anchor: فقال لم أعبد ربا لم تره العيون بمشاهدة العيان ولكن تراه القلوب بحقائق الإيمان

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: The report cites God's ungraspability by eyes and Moses' request: a manifestation to the mountain shattered it and made Moses fall unconscious; on revival, Moses repented of the claim that God is seen by eyes.
rows.anchor: وقوله لموسى { لن تراني ولكن انظر إلى الجبل فإن استقر مكانه فسوف تراني فلما تجلى ربه للجبل جعله دكا

rows.speaker: علي عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report in al-Tawhid says Moses was told that he could not see God in this world but would in the next; the mountain's collapse and Moses' swoon led him to affirm he was first among them to believe God is not seen.
rows.anchor: في الدنيا حتى تموت وتراني في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says both reports support his earlier argument: Moses asked about heart-vision, not impossible eyesight, which a prophet of his stature could not mistake.
rows.anchor: الروايتان - كما ترى - تؤيدان ما تقدم في البيان السابق
